summary: This informational document lists control-plane requirements for the Split Network Virtualization Edge architecture. In it, NVE functions are divided between a server and external network equipment. It describes what the control software on the server and the external equipment need from each other.

eli5.summary: A job is shared between a worker in the server and a helper box outside. This lists what they must tell each other to cooperate.

questions: what are the control plane requirements for split network virtualization edge
what happens to the network when a vm migrates
what is a tenant system interface
subtitle: What a hypervisor and its external network device must tell each other when virtual machines come, go and move.

tldr.problem: When the network virtualization edge (NVE) is split between a server and an external network device, the two halves need a control protocol to keep the network in step with virtual machines being created, moved and shut down.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC walks through the VM lifecycle, derives the signalling functions that follow (connect to a virtual network, associate and activate a tenant interface, and their reverses), and lists 13 requirements for the protocol.
tldr.outcome: It concludes that IEEE 802.1Q's VDP can serve as the protocol, with a few extensions, most importantly carrying Layer 3 addresses.

today: RFC 8394 is an Informational document published in May 2018. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and the metadata shows no later RFC replacing it.

sections.title: The Split-NVE Architecture
sections.content:
In the Split-NVE architecture the functions of a network virtualization edge (NVE) are divided between an end device that runs virtual machines and an external network device called the External NVE. The part on the end device is the tNVE (terminal-side) and the part on the External NVE is the nNVE (network-side). Overlay encapsulation and decapsulation are normally offloaded to the nNVE.

When the NVE sits inside the hypervisor, no standard protocol is needed because everything runs on one device. In the split case, one or more control-plane protocols are required so the hypervisor can hand the VM's networking state to the External NVE. The RFC says this protocol is internal to the NVE and runs between the tNVE and nNVE.

The document uses VMs as its example of a Tenant System, but notes that a service instance in a network appliance or a container is also one. Tenant Systems connect through a Tenant System Interface (TSI), and VLAN tags separate the traffic of different virtual networks between the tNVE and nNVE.
sections.eli5: The job of connecting a toy to the wider playground is shared: one helper sits in the toy box, and another stands outside. They need a way to talk.

sections.title: The VM Lifecycle
sections.content:
The VM states come from RFC 7666. The RFC picks out the events that matter to the External NVE.

  • Creation: the VM goes from preparing to shutdown to running. Its TSI should be associated with the External NVE before it enters the running state, preferably while shut down. If association fails, the VM should not go into the running state.
  • Live migration: the VM moves from running through migrating to shutdown on the source, and from shutdown through migrating to running on the destination. The destination External NVE must discover the TSI's addresses, its virtual network and its local VLAN ID before the VM runs. The VM should not be running on both hypervisors at once.
  • Termination: the External NVE deprovisions the VM and de-associates its TSI.
  • Pause and suspend: the External NVE should not de-associate a paused or suspended VM, since it can return to running at any time.
sections.eli5: A toy can be built, carried to another room, switched off, or put on pause. The helper at the door needs to know about each of these so it does not lock the wrong door.

sections.title: Signalling Functions
sections.content:
The RFC gives illustrative state machines and says they are not prescriptive. First, VN_Connect and VN_Disconnect tell the External NVE when an end device needs, or no longer needs, a virtual network. A protocol is preferred over static configuration because VN connectivity changes often as VMs come, move and go. The External NVE gives the end device a locally significant tag (such as a VLAN ID) for each connected VN. VN_Connect can be explicit, or implicit in the first TSI Associate message.

For each TSI there are three states: Init, Associated and Activated. Associate means the addresses are bound to a port and resources are reserved, but no traffic is allowed. Activate means traffic can flow, address mappings go into forwarding tables and filter rules are enabled. Addresses can be added, removed or updated in either state without changing the state.

The reverse messages undo this. A suspension can move a TSI from Activated back to Associated, a pause normally changes nothing, and a shutdown moves it to Init and releases all resources. The NVE can also learn tenant addresses by gleaning source addresses from received packets, or the hypervisor can signal them explicitly.
sections.eli5: First you book a seat, which holds your place but nobody may sit yet. Then you are called to sit, and the show can begin. Leaving works the same way in reverse.

sections.title: Protocol Requirements
sections.content:
Section 4 lists thirteen requirements, Req-1 to Req-13. The ones marked MUST are these:

  • Support a bridged network between end devices and the External NVE, and several end devices sharing one External NVE port (Req-1, Req-2).
  • Let either side start connecting or disconnecting a VN, with the end device able to request it and the External NVE able to request a disconnect (Req-5, Req-6).
  • Negotiate locally significant tags per VN (Req-7).
  • Let the end device associate, de-associate, activate or deactivate TSI addresses, and let the External NVE de-associate or deactivate them (Req-8, Req-9).
  • Let the end device add, remove or update addresses, in MAC, IP or IP-MAC pair form (Req-10).
  • Allow mutual authentication, and run over Layer 2 links (Req-11, Req-12).

Using several External NVEs at once is a MAY, either active-standby per VN (Req-3) or active-active for one VN (Req-4). Req-13 is a SHOULD: an end device should be able to say that an Associate or Activate came from a hot migration.
sections.eli5: This is the rule list for the conversation: both sides can say hello or goodbye, agree on a label for each group, and make sure the other side is who it claims to be.

sections.title: Using VDP
sections.content:
The VSI Discovery and Configuration Protocol (VDP) from IEEE 802.1Q can be the protocol between hypervisor and External NVE. VDP is carried over the Edge Control Protocol (ECP), which gives reliable transport over Layer 2. An EVB station is roughly a hypervisor, an EVB bridge is roughly the External NVE, and a VSI is roughly the virtual port a VM uses.

The RFC checks VDP against each requirement. Req-5, 6, 7, 9 and 12 are met. Req-1 to 4, 8, 10 and 13 are met partially and need extensions. For example, VDP must be able to send to a specific unicast MAC address, and it needs a new filter information format to carry IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. For Req-13, the M-bit and S-bit can signal migration or suspension, but a zero value is ambiguous, so that would need to be fixed. Req-11 is not met by VDP itself: the RFC prefers an out-of-band mechanism such as MACsec or 802.1X, though implicit authentication exists when the External NVE is directly connected.

The RFC's summary is that adding the ability to carry Layer 3 addresses lets VDP provide most of the functionality required.
sections.eli5: There is already a way for the toy box and the helper to talk. It almost does everything on the list, but it needs a few extra words, especially for street addresses.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
External NVEs must ensure that only authorized Tenant Systems join a virtual network. In some cases the tNVE must also authenticate the nNVE. If a secure channel is needed, existing mechanisms such as MACsec can be used, and authentication may be implicit when the nNVE sits in a bridge directly connected to the server.

Because the protocol changes configuration on both sides, implementations should log all state changes, significant protocol events and authentication results. There is also a design choice: the hypervisor can supply all the information the External NVE uses directly, which suits a trusted environment, or it can supply only a VN ID and a VM identifier, with the External NVE fetching authoritative details from a management system. The second gives more reliable information but is not always possible. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: The helper should only open doors for toys that really belong, so both sides check each other's names and write down everything that changes.
